plan.analysis: The constant seed attains 2/3, but a simple symmetric three-step tent [1,2,1] already gives R≈0.6736 by hand, and optimizing [1,c,1] gives ≈0.6778 near c≈1.65. So 2/3 is not the optimum. I am betting the best lower bound is a smooth symmetric unimodal step profile, with a possible asymmetric or multi-modal correction. The experiments test short symmetric families exactly, refine a fine symmetric profile by local optimization, and probe asymmetry/multi-modality by simulated annealing.

experiments.hypothesis: A short symmetric step profile with a raised center beats the constant; N=3 already improves to ≈0.6736, and optimizing the middle height gives ≈0.6778, so N=5,7,9 may improve further.
experiments.change: Search symmetric step arrays for N in {3,5,7,9}. For each N use variables h_0..h_floor((N-1)/2) with the mirror symmetry h_i=h_{N-1-i}; parameterize h_i=exp(u_i) and normalize the mean height to 1 inside the objective. Objective is -R(h), with R computed exactly from L=[0,*np.convolve(h,h),0] using the given formula. Use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead') from multiple starts: all-ones, the embedded tent [1,1.65,1], and 10 random log-normal perturbations. Keep the global best, loop over N/restarts until time.process_time() reaches 0.9*budget, and return the best heights (also comparing with start).
experiments.prediction: Best R will be strictly above 0.666667, around 0.677-0.680; increasing N beyond 3 may give a small additional gain.

experiments.hypothesis: A fine symmetric unimodal tent, with heights allowed to vary smoothly over many steps, will improve on the short three-step tent.
experiments.change: Use N=64 symmetric heights: variables u_0..u_31, set h_i=exp(u_i) for i<32 and h_i=h_{63-i}, then normalize mean height to 1. Minimize -R(h) with scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B', numerical gradients), where R is computed exactly from np.convolve. Use several starts: constant, tent h_i=1+0.8*(1-|2i/63-1|), and 5 random low-frequency cosine perturbations of the tent with amplitude 0.3. After each optimization, perturb the current best and rerun for the remaining time. Stop at 0.9*budget and return the best heights.
experiments.prediction: R will exceed 0.678, likely reaching 0.68-0.69, with a smooth central bump and positive nonuniform wings.

experiments.hypothesis: The optimal profile may be asymmetric or multi-modal; symmetric local searches could miss it, while simulated annealing with block moves can escape symmetric local optima.
experiments.change: Use N=32. Initialize from the better of start and an upsampled symmetric tent [1,1.65,1]. Run simulated annealing on the heights with exact R evaluation: proposals are (a) multiply one height by exp(eta*Z), (b) multiply a random contiguous block by exp(eta*Z), (c) swap two heights, with Z standard normal and eta around 0.35. Accept improvements always; accept worsening moves with probability exp(delta_R/T) with T decreased geometrically. Keep the best; every 2000 failed proposals restart from the best with a larger perturbation. Continue until time.process_time() reaches 0.9*budget, then return the best heights.
experiments.prediction: If asymmetry or multi-modality helps, this will find R above the best symmetric tent; otherwise it will stay near the symmetric result and support the symmetric optimum.

plan.analysis: The evidence is that higher R comes from flatter f*f tops (F6), and the algebra says why: if g=f*f is nearly constant, R≈1. The classic near-extremal choice is f(x)∝x^{-1/2} (or symmetric (x(1-x))^{-1/2}), whose autoconvolution is exactly constant on half the support; discretizing f_i∝(i+1/2)^{-1/2} with a finite end height should already give R≈0.90, well above 0.865. So the biggest expected gain is to change the shape family from a Gaussian bump to an endpoint-singular power law, then polish it. I bet on a singular left edge (asymmetric, consistent with F3/F6) plus a smooth modulation optimizing the decaying tail.

experiments.hypothesis: The Gaussian-bump seed is the wrong family; a discretized Beta/power singularity x^{-p} at one end makes f*f nearly constant on most of the support, so R should jump far above 0.865.
experiments.change: Replace the bump seeding block: for n in (200,400,800) and p in (0.35,0.5,0.65,0.8), build h_i = ((i+0.5)/n)^(-p), also a mirrored/right-singular version and a symmetric ((i+0.5)(n-i-0.5)/n^2)^(-p) version, clip the largest height to 1e3, evaluate exact R, keep the best; then run the existing hill-climbing/smoothing loop from that seed (still accepting the incoming `start` if better). Keep the deadline logic.
experiments.prediction: Best R ≥ 0.88, with p≈0.5 winning, confirming the x^{-1/2} mechanism; the reported profile will have max/mean ≫ 3.5 and one very tall edge step.

experiments.hypothesis: The optimal shape is a smooth modulation on top of a near-singular edge; a low-dimensional parametric family fitted directly will beat blind hill-climbing and reveal the tail shape.
experiments.change: At N=2000 build h_i = ((i+0.5)/N)^(-0.5) * exp(c0 + c1*u + c2*u^2 + c3*u^3 + c4*u^4) with u=(i+0.5)/N (5 coefficients), plus optional floor t: h = h + t. Optimize the 6 parameters with scipy.optimize.minimize (Nelder-Mead, then L-BFGS-B with numerical gradients) on -R, multi-start from the plain power law, from the resampled incoming `start`, and from a few random perturbations; iterate/restart from the best until 0.9*budget, keeping the best array (upsampled by interp to N=4000 for the final evaluation if it helps).
experiments.prediction: Fitted R at least 0.90, with the optimal modulation bending the tail upward (not pure x^{-1/2}) and t>0; the gain over experiment 1 shows the interior modulation matters.

experiments.hypothesis: p0005's N=400 shape is limited by resolution and by having no move that sharpens an edge; higher N plus explicit edge-sharpening and multi-scale log-block moves will find a better basin.
experiments.change: Upsample the incoming best to N=2000 by interpolation, then run the same random hill-climb with these changed moves only: (a) multiply a random log-uniform-width block by exp(N(0,s)) with s drawn from {0.02,0.1,0.3} per step, (b) an 'edge' move multiplying h[0] or h[-1] by 1.5 or 1/1.5, (c) the existing smoothing move at probability 0.1, (d) with probability 0.05 re-interpolate the current best to a random N in [1000,4000] before perturbing. Restart from the best (not cur) every 500 steps; keep the highest-R array seen; run to 0.92*budget.
experiments.prediction: R rises to 0.87–0.88 only (modest), showing resolution/edge moves help but the shape family, not the search, is the binding constraint — a useful negative control against experiments 1–2.

plan.analysis: p0012 (0.8808) is essentially x^{-1/2} times a mild quartic modulation, i.e. the algebraically predicted flat-autoconvolution edge, but it falls ~0.02 short of the ~0.90 algebra bound (F12). The three candidate causes are: the fixed exponent/degree-4 modulation is too stiff, finite-N quadrature, or the single-edge ansatz is structurally wrong. I bet on stiffness first (richer family, multi-N), then on a genuinely different search (free-form gradient in log-height space from p0012's basin, which p0013 never tried), and finally on a different structure (singularities at both ends) to test whether the single-edge mechanism is really optimal.

experiments.hypothesis: The 0.8808 plateau is caused by the family being too stiff: fixed exponent -0.5 and only a quartic log-modulation cannot bend the tail enough to shrink the f*f decay on [1,2]. A free exponent plus a degree-8 modulation, fitted at moderate N and re-scored at high N, will find a better tail.
experiments.change: In p0012's _build use params = (p, c0..c8, t): u=(i+0.5)/N; h = u**(-p) * exp(clip(sum_{k=0..8} c_k u**k, -60, 60)) + max(t,0), with p clipped to [0.05,1.5]. Fit at N=1200 with Nelder-Mead (maxfev 8000) then L-BFGS-B, multi-start from (a) p=0.5 plus a degree-8 polyfit of log(start*sqrt(u)) vs u, t=0, (b) p in {0.35,0.5,0.65}, zero poly, t=1e-3, (c) 0.05-scale random perturbations of the incumbent, restarting until 0.85*budget. Then rebuild the best params at N in {2000,4000,8000}, score each with _R, and return the best-scoring array (also compare the incoming start). Print best p, best R per N.
experiments.prediction: R >= 0.885 at some N; the optimum has p clearly different from 0.5 and nonzero c5..c8, confirming family stiffness (F12); if R stays <= 0.882 the family is not the bottleneck.

experiments.hypothesis: Any low-dimensional ansatz is the bottleneck. Directly optimizing all N heights in log-space, started inside p0012's singular-edge basin (never done: p0013's gradient run started from the Gaussian-bump basin), with an exact analytic gradient and FFT convolution, will escape the parametric family and push R toward the algebra bound.
experiments.change: Resample the incoming start (p0012's array) to N=2000 by linear interpolation, set y=log(h+1e-6). Minimize -R(exp(y)) with scipy L-BFGS-B using the analytic gradient: L=fftconvolve(h,h); S=h.sum(); num=(sum L^2 + sum L[:-1]*L[1:])/3; M=L.max(); den=S*S*M; g_j = (2L_j + L_{j-1} + L_{j+1})/3 - (num/den)*S*S*[j==argmax(L)] (zero-padded boundaries); grad_h = 2*correlate(g,h) implemented as np.convolve(g, h[::-1]) with the correct slice; grad_y = grad_h*h. Verify grad_y against finite differences at N=20 before the run. Optimize at N=2000 until 0.6*budget, then linearly upsample h to N=4000 and continue L-BFGS-B until 0.9*budget; return the best array over both resolutions and the start.
experiments.prediction: R >= 0.890, beating p0012 by >=0.009 and showing the parametric family was the limiter; if it stalls at <=0.882 the x^{-1/2} algebra bound is loose rather than the family.

experiments.hypothesis: The single left-edge singularity leaves a decaying f*f tail on the right half; adding a second, weaker singularity at the right end can flatten that tail and raise R. A two-edge power family nests the pure x^{-1/2} case, so it directly tests whether the one-sided mechanism is optimal.
experiments.change: Replace p0012's _build with h = a*u**(-p) + b*(1-u)**(-q) + c, u=(i+0.5)/N, params (p,q,a,b,c) with p,q clipped to [0.02,1.5], h clipped to 1e6. Optimize with Nelder-Mead (maxfev 6000) then L-BFGS-B on -R at N=2000, multi-start from (p,q,a,b,c) = (0.5,0.5,1,0,0), (0.5,0.5,1,1,0), (0.5,0.2,1,0.3,0), (0.3,0.7,1,0.5,0.01), plus 0.1-scale random perturbations of the incumbent, restarting until 0.85*budget. Rebuild the best params at N in {2000,4000,8000}, score each, return the best array (also compare the incoming start). Print best (p,q,a,b,c).
experiments.prediction: If a second edge helps, best R > 0.885 with q>0.1 and b>0; if best R <= 0.881 with b->0, the single x^{-1/2} edge is confirmed as the right structure and the F12 gap is stiffness/quadrature only.

plan.analysis: The singular-edge basin is locally saturated: four independent attacks on p0012 (richer family, free-form gradient, two-edge, multi-resolution) all land at 0.8808-0.8816, and p0015 (best, 0.881554) used only 8.3 s of its 30 s budget. p0019 reaches the same 0.881554 from a genuinely different shape (f*f peak at 0.364 vs p0015's 0.057), so the 0.8816 plateau may be a local max of the free-form problem, not the global one. Three untested levers: (a) a vanishing-right-edge family u^{-p}(1-u)^{+q}, which predicts a steeper f*f tail y^{1+2q} than the jump edge; (b) actually spending the full budget on randomized restarts; (c) resolving the singular edge with N=10000-20000, since the discrete score rewards a better-resolved spike (F18's open quadrature question). I bet modest gains (+0.001-0.004) live in one of the resolution/restart levers, and the structural (1-u)^q test settles the tail question.

experiments.hypothesis: p0019's two-edge shape ties p0015 at 0.881554 but sits in a different region (f*f peak at 0.364 vs 0.057), so its basin was never freely optimized. Also, a right edge that *vanishes* like (1-u)^q makes f*f decay as y^{1+2q} at x=2 (steeper than the linear jump-edge tail), which should raise R if the tail is the loss.
experiments.change: Replace p0019's family with h(u)=u^{-p}*(1-u)^{q}*exp(c0+c1 u+c2 u^2+c3 u^3+c4 u^4), u=(i+0.5)/N, with p,q each clipped to [0,1.5] and c's clamped; optimize (9 params) with multi-start Nelder-Mead then L-BFGS-B on -R at N=2000, then take the best array and run p0015-style free-form log-space L-BFGS-B (analytic gradient, N=2000 then 4000) for the final polish, keeping the best array overall.
experiments.prediction: If the vanishing right edge helps, best q* > 0 (0.1-0.5) and free-form-polished R >= 0.883; if q* -> 0 and R <= 0.882, the jump edge is optimal and the two-edge basin collapses onto the same local max.

experiments.hypothesis: 0.881554 may be a local max, not the global one: p0015 used only 8.3 of 30 s, and no experiment has run many perturbed restarts of the exact free-form objective from the singular-edge basin and kept a global best.
experiments.change: Keep p0015's _R_grad/_negR_grad and the N=2000->4000 L-BFGS-B, but after it, loop until 0.9*budget: (1) with prob 0.6 perturb best y by adding log-normal noise sigma=0.1-0.3 to a random contiguous block of heights (10-50% of N), otherwise to all heights; (2) re-run L-BFGS-B with maxiter 1500; (3) every few iterations upsample best to N=8000 and polish; (4) keep a running global best by exact R over all N tried. Return the global best array.
experiments.prediction: If 0.8816 is a local max, at least one restart exceeds 0.882 and reaches 0.883-0.885; if every restart returns to <=0.8816, the plateau is a strong attractor (near-global) and the loss is structural, not search.

experiments.hypothesis: F18 flags finite-N quadrature as untested: the f*f peak sits at 0.057 of support, near the coarsest part of the grid, and the discrete score rewards a better-resolved singular spike. p0015 stopped at N=4000; higher N with FFT-accelerated convolution should resolve the edge and raise R if quadrature is the limiter.
experiments.change: Replace np.convolve with scipy.signal.fftconvolve everywhere (both _R and the correlation step in _R_grad) to get O(N log N). Do not resample back down.
experiments.prediction: If limiting, R at N=10000 or 20000 exceeds 0.883 and keeps creeping with N; if it stays <=0.882, the continuum optimum is ~0.8816 and quadrature is not the bottleneck (F18 resolved negatively).
